metadata.title: A FOURIER-FREE DENSITY-INCREMENT PROOF OF ROTH’S THEOREM
metadata.abstract: We give an elementary, Fourier-free proof of Roth’s theorem. The proof follows Roth’s original density-increment strategy, but replaces the usual Fourier-analytic step with a direct combinatorial argument involving averages over sub-progressions. 1.Introduction In 1953, Roth proved that every subset of the integers of positive upper density contains a nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression. This can be stated in the following finite form. Theorem 1(Roth [ 8]).For every α> 0, if N is sufficiently large, then every set A⊂{ 0, 1,...,N− 1} with|A|≥αN contains a three-term arithmetic progressionx, x+r, x+ 2rwithr̸= 0. Roth’s theorem is a foundational result in density Ramsey theory; its extension to longer arithmetic progressions is a celebrated theorem of Sze- mer´ edi [9]. Proofs of Roth’s theorem have been given using quite different methods: Roth’s original proof is Fourier analytic [ 8]; Furstenberg proved Szemer´ edi’s theorem in full using ergodic-theoretic methods [2]; and graph- theoretic proofs of Roth’s theorem follow from the triangle removal lemma of Ruzsa and Szemer´ edi [7]. More combinatorial proofs have also been given using Szemer´ edi’s cube lemma [4] as well as using ideas related to the more general Hales–Jewett theorem [1]. There is also a rich history of quantitative improvements, which we do not attempt to summarize here; see [ 5, 6] for recent surveys. Roth’s original proof uses a density-increment argument. Starting with a set A⊂ [N] with no nontrivial three-term progressions, one proves that A has increased density on a long subprogression. Passing to that progression and rescaling, one repeats the argument. If the original interval is sufficiently long, the density would eventually have to exceed 1, providing a contradiction. The purpose of this note is to give a proof with the same density-increment structure, but without using Fourier analysis.
